deep.reconstruction:
The page is the opening of a draft of Ramanujan's 1915 paper 'On the integral ∫_0^x tan^{-1}t/t dt' (J. Indian Math. Soc. 7 (1915), 93–96; Collected Papers no. 4). Throughout, Φ(x)=∫_0^x arctan(t)/t dt. In modern notation this is Ti_2(x), the inverse tangent integral, and Φ(1)=G is Catalan's constant.

(1) Inversion formula. For x>0, Φ(x) − Φ(1/x) = (π/2) log x. [My fill-in] Differentiate: arctan(x)/x + x^{-2}·x·arctan(1/x) = (arctan x + arctan(1/x))/x = π/(2x). Both sides vanish at x=1.

(2) Power series. For |x|≤1, Φ(x) = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)^2. This follows by integrating the arctan series term by term divided by t.

Ramanujan says the following are proved 'by differentiating both sides with respect to x'.

(3) For 0<x<π/2: Σ_{k≥0} sin((4k+2)x)/(2k+1)^2 = Φ(tan x) − x log tan x.
- [Mine] The derivative of the RHS is x·sec²x/tan x − log tan x − x·sec²x/tan x = −log tan x.
- The derivative of the LHS is 2Σ cos((2k+1)2x)/(2k+1) = 2·(1/2) log cot x = −log tan x.
- As x→0+ both sides tend to 0.

(4) Take x=π/8 in (3), where tan(π/8)=√2−1 and the signs of sin((2k+1)π/4) are (+,+,−,−,…)·√2/2.
- This gives (√2/2)(1+1/3²−1/5²−1/7²+…) = Φ(√2−1) + (π/8) log(1+√2).
- Ramanujan's form √2(1−1/5²+1/9²−1/13²+…) = Φ(√2−1) + (π/8) log(1+√2) + π²/16 additionally uses [mine] the classical value L(2,χ_8) = 1−1/3²−1/5²+1/7²+… = π²/(8√2).
- Write A = Σ(−1)^k/(4k+1)² and B = Σ(−1)^k/(4k+3)². Then √2A − π²/16 = (√2/2)(A+B) + (√2/2)(A−B) − π²/16 = (√2/2)(A+B).
- So (4) is not a bare specialization: it is (3) plus an Euler/Bernoulli-type evaluation.

(5) Take x=π/12 in (3), where tan(π/12)=2−√3.
- [Mine] The coefficients of 1/n² (n odd) are 1/2·χ_4(n) for 3∤n and −χ_4(n) for 3|n.
- Hence the sum is (1/2)(10G/9) + G/9 = 2G/3.
- So 2G/3 = Φ(2−√3) + (π/12) log(2+√3), i.e. G = Φ(1) = (3/2)Φ(2−√3) + (π/8) log(2+√3).

(6) For 0<x<π/2: Σ_{k≥0} [(1/2)_k/k!]·(cos^{2k+1}x + sin^{2k+1}x)/(2k+1)² = Φ(tan x) + (π/2) log(2 cos x).
- [Mine] The LHS is F(cos x)+F(sin x) with F(y)=∫_0^y arcsin(t)/t dt.
- Its derivative is −(π/2 − x) tan x + x cot x = −(π/2) tan x + x/(sin x cos x), which equals the derivative of the RHS.
- At x→0 the LHS is F(1) = (π/2) log 2, matching the RHS.

(7) For 0<x<π/2: Σ_{n≥1} sin(nx) cos^n x/n² = Φ(tan x) + (π/2) log cos x − x log sin x.
- [Mine] The LHS is Im Li_2(z) with z = cos x·e^{ix} = (1+e^{2ix})/2, so 1−z = sin x·e^{i(x−π/2)}.
- The derivative is Im[−log(1−z)·z'/z] with z'/z = i − tan x. This gives −log sin x + (x − π/2) tan x, which equals the derivative of the RHS.
- Both sides tend to 0 at x→0+.

The last line begins a further theorem with a parameter α, valid for −π/2<x<π/2 and with 1 ≥ |(1−α) sin x| or |(1−1/α) cos x|. Its statement continues on the next folio, which goes on to infinite products and arctan sums evaluated via Φ(1) and Φ(e^{−πn/2}).
errors: No mathematical errors found in (1)–(7); all verified analytically above.

(4) is described as a 'particular case of (3)'. Strictly, (3) at x=π/8 gives (√2/2)(1+1/3²−1/5²−1/7²+…). Reaching Ramanujan's form √2(1−1/5²+1/9²−…) with the extra π²/16 also requires the classical value 1−1/3²−1/5²+1/7²+… = π²/(8√2), which is left implicit.
The hypothesis 0<x<π/2 is stated once before (6) and is meant to cover (7) as well. In (7) it is needed for log sin x and log cos x to be real.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript draft of Ramanujan's published 1915 paper on the inverse tangent integral. Formulas (1)–(7) appear there and in Notebooks Chapter 9 as edited by Berndt. The only point of interest is seeing the draft form; the content is well known as his.
